title: Living ashtpadi 4
hookLine: many say this stanza just before Ardas

cards: Near the end of a gurdwara service, the whole room rises. Shoes already off, heads already covered. People stand, palms pressed together, facing the Guru Granth Sahib.
Someone is about to lead the Ardas, the long standing prayer that closes the gathering. And in many gurdwaras, before the Ardas begins, the room says a stanza together.
Its first words came yesterday: too thaakur, tum peh ardaas. Yesterday it was a line in a book. Today, it's a room on its feet.

teach.b: The Ardas is the Sikh community's prayer. It remembers God, the ten Gurus and the Guru Granth Sahib; it remembers the Sikhs who suffered and served; then it asks, for the people present and for the good of all.
Most of the Ardas's wording isn't scripture. It grew up in the community and was set down in the Sikh code of conduct.

teach.h: BEFORE IT, THE GURU'S OWN WORDS.
teach.b: But the stanza many say just before it is scripture: the eighth stanza of Sukhmani's fourth ashtpadi, Guru Arjan's words from the Guru Granth Sahib. So the room moves from the Guru's words into the community's asking.
Why this stanza? Read it as a doorway. Too thaakur, tum peh ardaas: Master, to You, this prayer.

teach.h: THE ADDRESS, THE TERMS, THE TONE.
teach.b: That's the address on the envelope. Soul and body are all Your trust: that's who is asking, and on what terms. Nothing here is owned; all of it is held.

You are mother and father, we Your children: that's the tone. Not a petition to a distant court, but a child at home. Then: nobody knows Your limit, You are highest of the high, all creation is strung on Your thread.
Before anyone asks for anything, the stanza sets the size of things.

teach.h: THE ASKER IS SMALL, AND LOVED.
teach.b: The asker is small. The One asked is without end.
And the asker is still loved. That's ashtpadi four, lived in a room. The stanzas before say: you forgot the giver.
The last one says: turn around, stand up, and ask.

how: In many gurdwaras the congregation stands, palms together, facing the Guru Granth Sahib, and recites 'too thaakur tum peh ardaas' before the Ardas is led; many Sikhs also say it before their own Ardas at home.

o: a hymn of praise sung at sunrise
a prayer of asking, made to the One
a vow made before the whole sangat

p: the Guru's words said before it
trust, capital held for a while

s: the whole Ardas is a hymn from the Guru Granth Sahib
most of its wording grew up in the community; the stanza before it is scripture.
the congregation stands for the Ardas
the room rises, palms together, facing the Guru Granth Sahib.
'too thaakur' is the last stanza of Sukhmani's fourth ashtpadi
the eighth stanza, by Guru Arjan.

games.q: the room has risen. the Ardas is about to begin. what do many gurdwaras say first?
o: nothing: silence until the leader speaks.
games.why: many congregations say ashtpadi four's last stanza together, then the Ardas begins.

practice: If you're able, stand, with palms together or hands at rest.

If you pray, say the stanza's opening the way a gurdwara does, too thaakur, tum peh ardaas, jeeo pind sabh teree raas; if not, say the English slowly, You are the Master; soul and body are all Your trust, and notice how it feels said standing.
Then feel your feet on the floor, holding you up, and breathe.

wordCard.voice: Ardaas, a prayer of asking: the stanza that ends ashtpadi four, said by many Sikhs standing, just before the Ardas, the Guru's words, then the community's asking.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: ardaas, a prayer of asking; the stanza's own word, and the name of the Sikh standing prayer.

carryVoice: Your line: to you, this prayer. First the address, then the asking. Day four hundred fifty-three.
